caption:
Several Google DeepMind staff are quitting over Google's AI work for the military, the BBC reports.
Research engineer Sofia Liguori says seeing Google push AI into military operations made her "ashamed to work at Google."
Google says it follows a consistent contract review process and bans retaliation.

Should AI companies be able to say no to the military?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

slides.heading: Quitting over *the Pentagon*
paras: Sofia Liguori, a Google DeepMind research engineer in London, quit this week after three years, the BBC and The Intercept reported.
AI researcher Andreas Kirsch left earlier this month. Other staff told the BBC that more people are leaving.

slides.heading: *Any lawful* government purpose
paras: Earlier this year Google signed a Pentagon deal that lets its AI be used for classified military work, for "any lawful government purpose."
Kirsch said Google "seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI."

slides.heading: *Ashamed* to work at Google
paras: Liguori told the BBC that seeing Google push AI further into military operations made her "ashamed to work at Google."

paras.t: She wrote that AI for targeting makes it easier to escalate the brutality of war.

slides.heading: What *Google* says
paras: A Google spokesperson said the company works with public sector organizations worldwide and follows a consistent contract review process.
Google also said staff have channels to raise concerns and that its policies prohibit retaliation.

slides.hook: The fight over military AI is splitting Big Tech from the inside. Follow to see who leaves next.

site_article.headline: Google DeepMind staff resign in protest over the company's military AI contracts
site_article.dek: A London research engineer and an AI researcher have left, and other employees say more colleagues are following.
site_article.summary: Several Google DeepMind employees have resigned over Google's AI work for the military, according to the BBC and The Intercept. The departures follow a classified Pentagon contract that lets the government use Google's AI for any lawful purpose.
site_article.seo_title: Google DeepMind staff resign over Pentagon AI contracts
site_article.seo_description: Google DeepMind engineers are leaving in protest over a Pentagon deal that lets the military use Google's AI for classified work, the BBC reports.
site_article.answer_summary: Google DeepMind employees, including research engineer Sofia Liguori and AI researcher Andreas Kirsch, resigned in October 2026 over Google's contracts that allow its AI to be used for classified military work.
site_article.hero_alt: Portrait of former Google DeepMind research engineer Sofia Liguori, provided by her to The Intercept.

paragraphs.text: Several employees of Google DeepMind have resigned or are preparing to leave over Google's contracts to supply artificial intelligence for military work, the BBC and The Intercept reported on October 21, 2026. Both outlets spoke with Sofia Liguori, a research engineer based in London who left the company after about three years.

According to the BBC, AI researcher Andreas Kirsch also resigned earlier in October. The broadcaster said it spoke with several other current and former staff members who asked not to be named. One current employee told the BBC that some staff are leaving, and another said many people who feel strongly about the issue have already gone. Neither report gave a total number of departures.

In April 2026, Google signed a deal with the Pentagon that allows its AI to be used for classified military work, a contract first reported by The Information and later covered by Reuters. Under the agreement, the government can use Google's AI for any lawful government purpose, and Google cannot veto lawful operational decisions made by the government. Reuters said Google must also help adjust its safety settings and filters at the government's request.

The BBC noted that OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia and Reflection have signed similar agreements. Employees also pointed to Project Nimbus, the 2024 contract Google holds jointly with Amazon to provide cloud and AI services to the Israeli government and military, which the BBC said was reported to be worth $1.2 billion. Google said at the time that Nimbus was not directed at highly sensitive, classified or military workloads.

Liguori told the BBC that watching the company push AI further into military operations made her ashamed to work at Google, and she spoke on the record despite a contract that restricts public criticism. In a letter to colleagues described by The Intercept, she wrote that she no longer believes the company's technology will have a net positive impact on society and that using AI for targeting makes it easier to escalate the brutality of war.

The Intercept reported that Liguori joined DeepMind in 2023 and worked on using AI to route power through electrical grids. It said she took sick leave and holiday time in a protest the day after Google announced its classified Pentagon contract in April, and that she helped organize a demonstration outside the London office in February. Kirsch told the BBC that Google appears to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI.

Staff who spoke to the BBC said their contracts limit what they can say publicly and that some fear retaliation. Critics quoted in the report raised concerns about how much human oversight is possible when AI systems make recommendations at the speed of combat.

A Google spokesperson told both outlets that the company works with public sector organizations around the world and follows a consistent contract review process, which includes checking compliance with its acceptable use policies and AI principles. The company said employees have channels to raise concerns and that its policies prohibit retaliation. When the Pentagon deal was reported in April, Google said it remained committed to human oversight of AI used in surveillance and autonomous weapons.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the resignations show that the debate over military AI has moved from public statements to individual career decisions inside the labs that build the models. With most major AI companies now holding similar defense agreements, engineers who object have fewer employers to move to, which raises the stakes of every departure.
Watch whether more DeepMind researchers go public, and whether Google changes the review process or terms that govern how its models are used in classified military work.
